# Statement of Applicability

**GENERATED by tools/generate_statement_of_applicability.py — do not edit.**
Regenerate with `python tools/generate_statement_of_applicability.py`;
`tests/test_statement_of_applicability.py` fails if the committed file and the
generator disagree.

ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A, all 93 controls. For each: whether it applies, why,
and — where the software implements it — which rows of
[`COMPLIANCE_TRACKER.md`](COMPLIANCE_TRACKER.md) are the evidence. Those rows are
themselves asserted by tests, which is the point of citing them rather than
restating them: this document cannot claim something the register has not
verified, because the generator refuses to render if it does.

## Scope

Two things get conflated in a self-hosted product, and conflating them is how a
Statement of Applicability becomes untrue.

**This document is the SoA for the software** — what this repository builds and
ships, as a customer runs it in their own infrastructure. Every disposition below
answers for that.

**The adopting organisation needs its own**, covering its offices, its laptops,
its employment practices and its suppliers. No repository can contain that: this
one does not know the legal entity, the locations or the staff. Controls that
depend on those are marked `organisation` below and are the input to that
document, not a substitute for it.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| ISMS scope statement | `__ORGANISATION_TO_COMPLETE__` |
| Legal entity | `__ORGANISATION_TO_COMPLETE__` |
| Locations in scope | `__ORGANISATION_TO_COMPLETE__` |
| Information systems in scope | `__ORGANISATION_TO_COMPLETE__` |
| Exclusions from scope, with justification | `__ORGANISATION_TO_COMPLETE__` |
| Risk assessment this SoA follows | `__ORGANISATION_TO_COMPLETE__` (C2) |
| Approved by | `__ORGANISATION_TO_COMPLETE__` |
| Date of approval | `__ORGANISATION_TO_COMPLETE__` |

Those eight are deliberately blank. A generated SoA that filled in a scope
statement would be describing an organisation it knows nothing about — the same
refusal `RECORDS_OF_PROCESSING.md` makes about a legal basis.

## Dispositions

| Disposition | Count | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `product` | 29 | The software implements this. Cites register rows, every one of which must be `Verified`. |
| `shared` | 21 | The software does a defined part; the organisation must do the rest. Both are stated. |
| `operator` | 15 | A decision in the customer's own deployment or facility. |
| `organisation` | 27 | The adopting organisation's to do. No code can. |
| `excluded` | 1 | Does not apply, with the reason. Never used to mean "not done yet". |

50 of the 93 controls have something in this software behind them. That is not a score: most of Annex A is about people, places
and paperwork, and a product claiming most of it would be claiming things it
cannot see. The number worth reading is the 2 marked `excluded` — a control
declared not applicable is the only kind an auditor argues with.

## A.5 Organizational controls (37)

| Control | Title | Applies | Evidence | Justification |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 5.1 | Policies for information security | `organisation` | — | OR-2. Policy documents are the organisation's to write and sign. What the software contributes is that several policies would otherwise be unenforceable claims: the access-control policy is asserted by AC-1 to AC-11, and the cryptography policy by DP-1 and DP-2. |
| 5.2 | Information security roles and responsibilities | `organisation` | — | Named people. The register carries an owner per control, which is the input, not the assignment. |
| 5.3 | Segregation of duties | `organisation` | — | The mechanism exists — AC-3 gates every privileged action on an admin role and AC-2 keeps organisations apart — but deciding which person holds which role is the organisation's. |
| 5.4 | Management responsibilities | `organisation` | — | Management's own commitment. |
| 5.5 | Contact with authorities | `organisation` | — | Who notifies which regulator, and within what window. GDPR Art. 33 is 72 hours; the audit trail (LG-1) is what makes a notification factual rather than a guess. |
| 5.6 | Contact with special interest groups | `organisation` | — | Memberships and mailing lists. |
| 5.7 | Threat intelligence | `shared` | `CM-2`, `CM-3` + `__ORGANISATION_TO_COMPLETE__` | The software ingests the part that can be automated: dependency advisories on every build (CM-2) and image CVEs (CM-3), both gating. Human threat intelligence — sector advisories, an attacker who is interested in this customer — is the organisation's. |
| 5.8 | Information security in project management | `organisation` | — | How work is planned. `docs/COMPLIANCE_TRACKER.md` and `docs/REVIEW_FINDINGS.md` are evidence that security work is tracked, not a policy that it must be. |
| 5.9 | Inventory of information and other associated assets | `shared` | `DP-9` + `__ORGANISATION_TO_COMPLETE__` | For the data this software holds the inventory is complete and asserted: DP-9 covers all 106 classified personal-data columns across 20 tables plus the one JSON payload, generated from the live schema so a migration cannot outdate it. Assets beyond that data — hosts, laptops, accounts — are the organisation's. |
| 5.10 | Acceptable use of information and other associated assets | `organisation` | — | A rule about people, not a mechanism. |
| 5.11 | Return of assets | `organisation` | — | Offboarding. The software's half is that access can actually be withdrawn — AC-11, three levers including revocation of the credential itself. |
| 5.12 | Classification of information | `product` | `DP-9`, `DP-8` | Every column of every personal-data table is classified, and the classification is a rule rather than a list: F115 asserts it against the live schema, so a new column fails the build until somebody decides what it is. |
| 5.13 | Labelling of information | `excluded` | — | The software stores structured records in named columns, not documents that could carry a classification label. There is no artefact here to label. Labelling of the organisation's own documents belongs to its own SoA. |
| 5.14 | Information transfer | `shared` | `DP-5` + `__ORGANISATION_TO_COMPLETE__` | The server does not transfer information out of the customer's network — DP-5, asserted by a source scan and a runtime test in each repository after two outbound calls were found. The client's update checks and web tools reach the internet by default and are all off under `air_gapped: true`, which the organisation decides. In-transit protection of the traffic it does carry is DP-4, which is `Operator`: the product ships a TLS terminator but the DNS record and the certificate's trust chain are the customer's. Transfers the organisation chooses to make from its own systems are its own. |
| 5.15 | Access control | `product` | `AC-1`, `AC-2`, `AC-3`, `AC-7`, `AC-10` | Authentication on every route, organisation scoping swept from the live router, and admin-only gating on privileged actions. Account existence is not disclosed to an anonymous caller either (AC-10), which is the part of access control that leaks before anyone is authenticated. |
| 5.16 | Identity management | `product` | `AC-4`, `AC-9` | No standing or default accounts (AC-4), and identities either local or from the customer's IdP over OIDC (AC-9). |
| 5.17 | Authentication information | `product` | `AC-5`, `AC-6`, `AC-1` | Passwords bcrypt-hashed, one-time codes rate-limited and constant-time compared, and no credential in a URL. |
| 5.18 | Access rights | `product` | `AC-7`, `AC-8`, `AC-11` | Granted on authorisation (AC-7), reviewed periodically (AC-8), and revocable three ways — deactivation, credential withdrawal, deletion (AC-11). |
| 5.19 | Information security in supplier relationships | `organisation` | — | OR-4. The product's own supplier surface is unusually small and is stated: no sub-processors, because nothing leaves the deployment (DP-5). |
| 5.20 | Addressing information security within supplier agreements | `organisation` | — | Security clauses in the organisation's own supplier contracts. OR-4. Worth noting what is *not* needed here: no Article 28 processor agreement with this vendor, because no data reaches it (DP-5) and there is therefore no processing to contract for. |
| 5.21 | Managing information security in the ICT supply chain | `shared` | `CM-8`, `CM-2`, `CM-3`, `CM-11` + `__ORGANISATION_TO_COMPLETE__` | The software's supply chain is asserted: an SBOM per release (CM-8), dependency auditing (CM-2), image scanning (CM-3), and a declared licence (CM-11). Suppliers the organisation contracts with are its own. |
| 5.22 | Monitoring, review and change management of supplier services | `organisation` | — | Review of the organisation's suppliers. OR-4. |
| 5.23 | Information security for use of cloud services | `operator` | — | The customer chooses the cloud and configures it. What the software guarantees is that the choice stays theirs: nothing phones home, and the marketplace deployments run entirely in their project (DP-5). |
| 5.24 | Information security incident management planning and preparation | `organisation` | — | LG-8, and the largest remaining gap in the register. The prerequisite is built — an immutable audit trail (LG-1, LG-2), a reviewable and exportable one (LG-4), and alerting (LG-7) — but a plan naming people and steps is not something code produces. C4. |
| 5.25 | Assessment and decision on information security events | `shared` | `LG-1`, `LG-3`, `LG-6` + `__ORGANISATION_TO_COMPLETE__` | The software decides which events are worth recording and refuses to lose them: every privileged mutation, every authentication attempt including failures, and a write failure that is itself counted and alerted. Triage of what those events mean is the organisation's. |
| 5.26 | Response to information security incidents | `shared` | `AC-11`, `DP-2` + `__ORGANISATION_TO_COMPLETE__` | The levers a response needs exist and are demonstrated: withdraw one person's sessions, deactivate a membership, rotate the encryption key with both keys live, take a node out of rotation. Who pulls them, and when, is the plan in C4. |
| 5.27 | Learning from information security incidents | `organisation` | — | The pre-production review (`docs/REVIEW_FINDINGS.md`) is exactly this for defects rather than incidents — each one what was found, what it cost, and the rule that keeps it fixed. The practice for real incidents needs the plan first. |
| 5.28 | Collection of evidence | `product` | `LG-2`, `LG-4` | The audit trail is append-only in the database rather than by convention: `UPDATE` is refused by a trigger, demonstrated, and the refusal survives a restore — re-tested by the drill in F5. Exportable as JSON Lines for a SIEM. |
| 5.29 | Information security during disruption | `shared` | `AV-1`, `DP-10`, `DP-11` + `__ORGANISATION_TO_COMPLETE__` | The software degrades rather than cascading (AV-1) and its backups are restorable, proven by a drill that runs in CI using the shipped script (DP-10, DP-11). A continuity plan for the organisation is separate. |
| 5.30 | ICT readiness for business continuity | `shared` | `DP-10`, `DP-11` + `__ORGANISATION_TO_COMPLETE__` | Recovery of the software is exercised: dump, restore, compare, and boot the application on the restored database. The recovery-time objective and who declares a disaster are the organisation's. |
| 5.31 | Legal, statutory, regulatory and contractual requirements | `organisation` | — | Which regimes apply to this organisation. The software supplies what GDPR asks of it: records of processing, subject access, erasure and retention. |
| 5.32 | Intellectual property rights | `product` | `CM-11` | The software declares its own licence where tooling reads it — both images said `NOASSERTION`, the SPDX string for "nobody said", and there was no LICENSE file at all. |
| 5.33 | Protection of records | `product` | `LG-2`, `DP-6`, `DP-1`, `DP-2` | Audit records cannot be altered (LG-2) and are retained by a runner that applies the configured window rather than merely offering the setting (DP-6). Provider credentials among those records are encrypted at rest with a rotatable key (DP-1, DP-2). |
| 5.34 | Privacy and protection of PII | `product` | `DP-9`, `DP-8`, `DP-7`, `DP-6`, `DP-13` | Records of processing generated from the schema (DP-9), subject access covering every classified column (DP-8), erasure that redacts a named person without destroying other contributors' history (DP-7), retention applied (DP-6), and a feature removed outright because it collected data the deployment could not use (DP-13). |
| 5.35 | Independent review of information security | `organisation` | — | OR-5, OR-7. An auditor, and an observation window. |
| 5.36 | Compliance with policies, rules and standards for information security | `shared` | `CM-1` + `__ORGANISATION_TO_COMPLETE__` | Unusually strong on the software side, and worth stating precisely: the register itself is asserted by tests — every finding it cites exists, every status is from the vocabulary, the summary counts match, and no absence claim may name a control the register has marked `Verified`. Compliance of people with policy is the organisation's. |
| 5.37 | Documented operating procedures | `shared` | `CM-10` + `__ORGANISATION_TO_COMPLETE__` | `docs/self-hosting.md`, `docs/gpu-clusters.md`, the chart's README and the backup script's own header document how to run it, and `make check-configs` plus the kind install assert that the documented procedures work. The organisation's internal procedures are its own. |

## A.6 People controls (8)

| Control | Title | Applies | Evidence | Justification |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 6.1 | Screening | `organisation` | — | Employment. Nothing in a repository can do this. |
| 6.2 | Terms and conditions of employment | `organisation` | — | Employment contracts stating security responsibilities. Nothing in a repository can create an obligation on a person. |
| 6.3 | Information security awareness, education and training | `organisation` | — | OR-3, and the register's only People row. Training is delivered to people by people; the closest the software comes is refusing unsafe configuration at startup rather than relying on somebody having been taught not to set it. |
| 6.4 | Disciplinary process | `organisation` | — | A process for responding to a person's breach of policy. The software's contribution is evidence rather than process: an append-only audit trail that says who did what (LG-1, LG-2). |
| 6.5 | Responsibilities after termination or change of employment | `shared` | `AC-11` + `__ORGANISATION_TO_COMPLETE__` | The technical half is built and was the subject of three findings in this review: deactivation takes effect on the next request, a credential can be withdrawn outright, and deletion ends every session it issued. The process around offboarding is the organisation's. |
| 6.6 | Confidentiality or non-disclosure agreements | `organisation` | — | Agreements with staff and third parties. The product reduces how much is disclosed in the first place — nothing leaves the deployment, so no vendor NDA covers customer data here (DP-5). |
| 6.7 | Remote working | `organisation` | — | A policy about people and their devices. |
| 6.8 | Information security event reporting | `shared` | `LG-7`, `DP-11` + `__ORGANISATION_TO_COMPLETE__` | The software reports events it can see — nine metrics, eight alert rules shipped with the chart, and a red healthcheck when a backup goes stale. A person reporting something they noticed needs a channel, which is the organisation's. |

## A.8 Technological controls (34)

| Control | Title | Applies | Evidence | Justification |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8.1 | User endpoint devices | `organisation` | — | Developer laptops. The one thing the software controls here is what it puts on them, and that is asserted: the desktop app's webview is confined by a CSP that permits no remote origin in any directive, after a first attempt allowed `connect-src https:`. |
| 8.2 | Privileged access rights | `product` | `AC-3`, `AC-7` | Every privileged action is admin-gated, and the sweep is generated from the live router rather than from a list of endpoints. |
| 8.3 | Information access restriction | `product` | `AC-2`, `AC-7` | Organisation scoping on every parametrised portal endpoint, swept; and B7 closed the one authorisation path that decided on the git provider alone without asking whether the person was still a member. |
| 8.4 | Access to source code | `shared` | `AC-5`, `DP-5` + `__ORGANISATION_TO_COMPLETE__` | The software's own handling of a customer's source is the part it can answer for: source passes through to the model endpoint the customer chose and is not stored, and credentials never appear in a response. Repository access is CodeIndex's; access to *this* repository is the organisation's. |
| 8.5 | Secure authentication | `product` | `AC-1`, `AC-5`, `AC-6`, `AC-9` | Bcrypt passwords, rate-limited one-time codes, OIDC with PKCE and pinned algorithms, and no token in a URL — the last of which was found twice, in two repositories. |
| 8.6 | Capacity management | `product` | `AV-1`, `LG-7` | The connection pool is sized against the server and says so at startup, exhaustion is counted and alerted rather than surfacing as unexplained 500s, and a burst degrades instead of cascading. |
| 8.7 | Protection against malware | `shared` | `CM-3` + `__ORGANISATION_TO_COMPLETE__` | The software's own artefacts are scanned every build and the build fails on a HIGH or CRITICAL finding (CM-3). Endpoint anti-malware on the organisation's machines is its own. |
| 8.8 | Management of technical vulnerabilities | `shared` | `CM-2`, `CM-3`, `CM-8` + `__ORGANISATION_TO_COMPLETE__` | Detection is automated and gating: dependency auditing, image scanning, and an SBOM so a customer can answer "what is in this" without asking. How fast a finding must be fixed is a commitment, not a mechanism — CM-9, and C6. |
| 8.9 | Configuration management | `product` | `CM-5`, `CM-10`, `CM-6`, `CM-4` | Unsafe configuration is refused at startup rather than warned about, the chart refuses ten inputs rather than defaulting them, and the deployment artefact is now installed on a real cluster in CI — which found that it never could have been. Every container runs as a non-root user with a read-only root filesystem and dropped capabilities (CM-4). |
| 8.10 | Information deletion | `product` | `DP-6`, `DP-7`, `AC-11` | Retention applied by a runner (DP-6), erasure that redacts a named person from stored payloads without destroying other contributors' history (DP-7), and account deletion that ends every session the account issued (AC-11). |
| 8.11 | Data masking | `product` | `LG-5`, `LG-9` | Logs carry no personal data they do not need — enforced by an AST rule over all of `app/`, after the chat endpoint was found logging the prompt — and error responses disclose nothing about the system. |
| 8.12 | Data leakage prevention | `product` | `DP-5`, `LG-5`, `LG-9` | The strongest claim in this document, and the most tested: nothing leaves the deployment for the vendor. Two outbound calls were found and put behind a switch, a source scan and a runtime test in each repository defend it, and the desktop webview is confined by a CSP that permits no remote origin. Error responses disclose nothing either (LG-9), after an anonymous sign-up received 484 characters of database error naming every column of `users`. |
| 8.13 | Information backup | `product` | `DP-10`, `DP-11` | Backups are taken by a shipped script that verifies each archive before counting it and prunes only after a success, and they are restorable — a drill that runs in CI with that same script, comparing schema, rows, encrypted credentials byte for byte, sequences, and the append-only trigger. |
| 8.14 | Redundancy of information processing facilities | `operator` | — | Replica counts, multi-zone scheduling and a standby database are the customer's topology. The software is stateless per process and horizontally scalable, and the chart exposes the replica counts. |
| 8.15 | Logging | `product` | `LG-1`, `LG-3`, `LG-6`, `LG-2` | One audit event per privileged request, by a middleware rule over the live router rather than a call in each handler; authentication attempts including failures; and a write that fails is counted and alerted rather than lost quietly. The records cannot be altered once written (LG-2), enforced by a database trigger rather than by convention. |
| 8.16 | Monitoring activities | `product` | `LG-7`, `LG-4` | Ten metrics and eight alert rules shipped with the chart, every alerted metric asserted to exist and every metric asserted to have a rule, and labels allowlisted so none can carry personal data. The customer runs the monitoring; nothing phones home. |
| 8.17 | Clock synchronization | `product` | `LG-7`, `AC-11` | Added by B8, which found this control was load-bearing and unmeasured. Session revocation compares a token's `iat` against a watermark, and with both taken from app clocks a replica five seconds ahead minted tokens that survived a withdrawal — demonstrated. The watermark comes from the database now, and the remaining app-to-database gap is sampled every minute, published as `igni_clock_skew_seconds` and alerted on by `IgniClockSkew`. The audit trail's ordering and retention's windows depended on the same clocks. |
| 8.18 | Use of privileged utility programs | `shared` | `CM-4`, `CM-10` + `__ORGANISATION_TO_COMPLETE__` | The software ships none: containers run as a non-root user with a read-only root filesystem and dropped capabilities, and no pod mounts a service-account token. Utilities an operator installs on the host are theirs. |
| 8.19 | Installation of software on operational systems | `product` | `CM-1`, `CM-10`, `CM-7` | Images are pinned by digest-bearing tags rather than `latest`, which the chart refuses; migrations run as a pre-install hook that must succeed before anything serves; and CD cannot build an untested commit. |
| 8.20 | Networks security | `shared` | `CM-10` + `__ORGANISATION_TO_COMPLETE__` | The chart ships a NetworkPolicy and a TLS terminator, and B2 found the Caddyfile it shipped had never started — `caddy validate` rejected it from the day it was written. Both are validated in CI now. The network the customer runs it on is theirs, and DP-4 is `Operator` for the parts that genuinely are — the DNS record, and TLS anywhere they put their own proxy in front. |
| 8.21 | Security of network services | `shared` | `AC-1` + `__ORGANISATION_TO_COMPLETE__` | The services the software exposes are enumerated and each is authenticated: user tokens, organisation-scoped tokens for services a super admin has approved, a node token, and a super-admin key. B7 found a service-token subtree unreachable at the URL its clients used, in both directions; that subtree and its shared secret have since been replaced by service registration and approval. Transport protection of those services is DP-4, `Operator`. |
| 8.22 | Segregation of networks | `operator` | — | The chart's NetworkPolicy segregates what it can inside a namespace; the surrounding network design is the customer's. |
| 8.23 | Web filtering | `shared` | `DP-5` + `__ORGANISATION_TO_COMPLETE__` | The server makes no request to the web (DP-5). The client's agent has two web tools, a fetch that is allowed by default and a search that asks first, and both are off under `air_gapped: true`, `permissions.web_fetch: deny` and `permissions.web_search: deny`, which an organisation can publish as group policy. Which sites a deployment that keeps them on may reach is the organisation's own proxy and its own SoA. |
| 8.24 | Use of cryptography | `product` | `DP-1`, `DP-2`, `AC-5` | Fernet for provider credentials at rest, with a missing key refusing the write rather than storing plaintext; rotation with both keys live and a tool that reports before it writes; bcrypt for passwords; and pinned JWT algorithms. TLS ships as a terminator but is cited as DP-4 `Operator` rather than as evidence here, because the certificate and the DNS record are the customer's — the first version of this document claimed it and the generator refused to render. |
| 8.25 | Secure development life cycle | `shared` | `CM-1` + `__ORGANISATION_TO_COMPLETE__` | CI gates lint, types, a security audit, the whole server suite, the portal suite, both browser suites, an accessibility pass over every page, a chart install on a real cluster and a restore drill. A count of tests is deliberately not quoted here: a number in a generated document is the staleness this file exists to avoid. The policy that says all of this must happen is OR-2. |
| 8.26 | Application security requirements | `shared` | `CM-1` + `__ORGANISATION_TO_COMPLETE__` | This register is the requirement set, and it is asserted rather than asserted-to: every control cites evidence, and the review sections indexed in `REVIEW_FINDINGS.md` record what each requirement cost. Requirements the organisation adds are its own. No count is quoted: the first version derived one, which meant writing a new section made this document stale — a coupling that bought nothing, since the claim is that the record exists and not how long it is. |
| 8.27 | Secure system architecture and engineering principles | `product` | `DP-5`, `CM-4`, `CM-5`, `AC-2` | Stated and enforced rather than aspirational: no data leaves the deployment, no pod runs as root, unsafe configuration is refused at startup, and authorisation is checked at one choke point per question so a new route cannot forget. |
| 8.28 | Secure coding | `product` | `CM-1`, `CM-2` | Static analysis and typing gate every change, and the recurring pattern of this review is that a fix ships as a rule over the live router or the live schema rather than as a corrected call site — because a list of call sites rots. |
| 8.29 | Security testing in development and acceptance | `product` | `CM-1`, `AC-2`, `AC-11` | Security behaviour is tested, not reviewed: cross-organisation access swept across every parametrised endpoint, revocation swept across every authenticated route, an air-gap rule in both repositories, and every fix in this review revert-checked to prove the test fails without it. |
| 8.30 | Outsourced development | `organisation` | — | Who writes the code. If development is outsourced, the gates in CM-1 apply to their commits identically — that is the point of gating in CI rather than in review. |
| 8.31 | Separation of development, test and production environments | `product` | `CM-6`, `CM-5` | Separated, and the separation is enforced rather than conventional: production refuses the dev authentication bypass, `/docs` and `/redoc` 404, and the bypass's durable side effect — a live admin row that outlived the flag — is refused at startup. |
| 8.32 | Change management | `product` | `CM-7`, `CM-1` | Migrations are reversible and round-trip tested against populated data, CD cannot build an untested commit, and the chart's migration hook must succeed before anything serves. |
| 8.33 | Test information | `product` | `CM-6`, `DP-13` | No production data in tests: fixtures are synthetic, and the one dev affordance with a durable side effect was found by reading a restored backup and then refused at startup. |
